contract.proves:
A desired-state mutation attempted while etcd cannot write must be atomic:
committed, or rejected. Never half-published.

THE FAULT. Exhaust etcd's backend QUOTA, then attempt a real desired-state
change, then release it.

WHY QUOTA AND NOT A FULL DISK. The first version of this filled the filesystem
etcd writes to. That directory lives on the HOST root filesystem via a docker
volume, so "leave 2 MB free" meant writing ~57 GB to the developer's disk — and
the only reason it did not is that it timed out first. Filling someone's disk to
test a cluster property is not an acceptable trade at any speed.
Quota exhaustion is also the faithful fault: the 2026-08-16 outage was
quota-backend-bytes exceeded, not a full disk.

WHY THIS IS NOT disk-pressure-detection. That scenario fills the node's root
disk and checks the cluster NOTICES. This makes etcd refuse writes and attempts
a mutation into that refusal — so the question is not detection but atomicity.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY. The 2026-08-16 outage was an etcd NOSPACE
event: the backend hit quota and the control plane went read-only. What was
never established is what happens to a mutation caught in that window. A
desired-state write is not one key: it is a record, a generation, and the
reconcile that follows. A partial write leaves the cluster pointed at something
nobody chose, and — worse — leaves no error for the operator to act on, because
from the caller's side the command simply failed.

THE TWO ACCEPTABLE OUTCOMES, and there is no third:

    the mutation never happened      — refused, nothing changed
    the mutation completed exactly once

There is no acceptable state called "the record is there but the generation is
not", and none called "the command failed but the write landed".

WHAT MUST HOLD. After the space is released, the cluster returns to healthy
with no standing alarms, no ambiguous or half-published artifacts, and desired
state coherent — whichever of the two outcomes occurred.
